Examples & Scenarios

Abbreviations used on this page (TSDB, WAL, TTL, HWM, XPUB, ZMQ, SQLite, JSON, CLI, API, RSS, fd, PEP, CORS, OBS...) are defined in the Abbreviations & jargon section.

Each section shows a real-world task with complete code you can copy and run. Every example assumes sqtseries is running on 127.0.0.1 with its default ports. If you have not installed it yet, start with the Quick Start.

Ready-to-run scripts. The examples/ directory in the project repository contains standalone scripts for every operation described below. They run against any sqtseries instance — most accept --host and port-specific flags (e.g. --write-port, --query-port, --http-port). Run them with python3 examples/<name>.py.

The camera pipeline lives in its own subdirectory, examples/camera/: overlay_server.py (simulated camera-metrics WebSocket source that also serves a live dashboard page), overlay.html (that dashboard — subscribes to the same-origin metrics WebSocket and renders readings as they arrive), camera_feed.py (pump a camera feed into sqtseries and answer every question the data can answer), sqtcam.sh (one-command runner: sqtseries + simulator + feed in a tmux session, for overnight data collection), and conn_validate.py (validate the live connection/subscription feed).

Available scripts: run_custom.py (start/verify/stop your own instance with your own config, ports, and database), producer.py (ZMQ ingestion), ingest_http.py (HTTP ingestion), consumer.py (ZMQ/HTTP query), query_examples.py (every query type), question_examples.py (13 classic questions answered end to end, each with machine-readable output), question_examples_advanced.py (10 advanced questions: per-series, percentiles, trends, data quality, staleness, and more), stream_examples.py (live subscription), admin_examples.py (all 9 admin commands), stats_monitor.py (live stats feed), maintenance_examples.py (backup, vacuum, health loop), tags_examples.py (why tags exist, whole-metric vs per-tag queries, cardinality).

The question catalog. Start with question_examples.py: it seeds deterministic sample data and answers the classic questions people ask — averages, yesterday's peak, 99th percentiles, counts, trends, buckets, busiest hour/day, sums, staleness, all-time stats, and HTTP/curl variants — printing each answer as a machine-readable ANSWER: key = value line. A short note: the demo seeds "history" (yesterday, last week), so start the service with the clock-skew guard raised: [ingestion] reject_client_timestamp_skew_s = 864000 (10 days).

0. Running the service with your own config, ports, and database

Every example below assumes sqtseries is running on the default ports. When you want your own ports or your own database file, the one command that starts it is (global options like --config and --db come before the run subcommand):

sqtseries --config /etc/sqtseries/config.toml run
# identical with python -m (what the examples/ scripts and systemd use):
python3 -m sqtseries --config /etc/sqtseries/config.toml run

Pick any ports, DB path, etc. in the config — see Configuration. To choose only the database on the command line: sqtseries --db /data/tsdb.sqlite run.

The script examples/run_custom.py walks the full cycle for you: it writes a config with free ports and a fresh database file, starts the service with --config … run, waits for the admin ping, writes and queries one metric over those ports, then stops the service — and on each step prints the exact command it ran, so you can copy it line by line:

python3 examples/run_custom.py

To register the service with systemd instead, the unit embeds the same config (plus the database path as an environment variable) — install it with the global --config flag:

sqtseries --config /etc/sqtseries/config.toml install   # user unit
sqtseries --config /etc/sqtseries/config.toml install --system  # system unit

0a. Script reference: every example and its options

Most scripts accept --host (default 127.0.0.1) and the port flag(s) listed below, so they work against any sqtseries instance — including one running on custom ports (run_custom.py and camera/overlay_server.py are the exceptions: they manage their own ports). Unless stated otherwise, scripts connect to an already-running service and exit on their own; the ones marked streaming run until Ctrl+C.

ScriptPurposeOptions (default)Runs until
producer.py Send measurements via ZMQ PUSH --port 12501, --rate 10 msg/s (0 = as fast as possible), --count 0 (0 = forever), --batch 500 (checkpoint print) — count sent or forever
ingest_http.py Send measurements via HTTP (no ZMQ needed) --port 12505, --rate 2 msg/s, --batch 20 points per request, --count 0 (0 = forever) — count sent or forever
consumer.py Run a query over ZMQ or HTTP --port 12502 (ZMQ query), --http base URL (e.g. http://127.0.0.1:12505) — one query
query_examples.py Every query type: raw, whole-window agg, downsampling, multi-agg, HTTP --write-port 12501, --query-port 12502, --http-port 12505 — seeds data, then runs
question_examples.py 13 classic questions answered (question catalog) --write-port 12501, --query-port 12502, --http-port 12505 — seeds data, then runs
stream_examples.py Live measurements (ZMQ SUB, Python client, or WebSocket) positional topic prefix (* = all), --port 12503, --http-port 12505 (for --ws), --ws, --client streaming — Ctrl+C
admin_examples.py Every admin command (ping → vacuum) --port 12504 — one pass
stats_monitor.py Live stats PUB events (conn/sub/report) positional filter prefix (conn, sub, report, or empty = all), --port 12506 streaming — Ctrl+C
maintenance_examples.py Health check, stats, backup, optimize, vacuum --admin-port 12504, --http-port 12505, --backup-only, --health-loop N seconds (0 = run once) — one pass (or loop with Ctrl+C)
question_examples_advanced.py 10 advanced questions: per-series breakdowns, percentiles, trends, data quality, staleness --write-port 12501, --query-port 12502, --http-port 12505, --admin-port 12504, --db PATH (needed for the per-series questions) — seeds data, then runs
run_custom.py Start, verify, and stop your own instance (writes a config, picks free ports, runs python3 -m sqtseries --config … run) --workdir (default sqt-custom-work) — full lifecycle, then exits

camera/overlay.html Live dashboard served by the simulator at / and /overlay.html — subscribes to the same-origin /ws/metrics WebSocket and renders each reading as it arrives, with auto-reconnect; add ?sqtseries=ws://…/ws/subscribe to also stream what the time-series database publishes ?sqtseries= WS URL to sqtseries, &metric= topic prefix filter — stays live while the tab is open

camera/sqtcam.sh One-command runner: starts sqtseries, the overlay simulator, and the camera feed in a three-window tmux session for long data collection — (uses /tmp/sqtcam/conf.toml; refuses to start a second session) — runs until tmux kill-session -t sqtcam
camera/conn_validate.py Validate the live connection/subscription feed of a running sqtseries: joins/leaves WebSocket + ZMQ subscribers and asserts exact counts, arrival/leaving times, and push latency --http-port 12505, --stream-port 12503, --clients 3, --zmq-subs 2, --timeout 5 — one pass (exits non-zero on any mismatch)

Note: question_examples.py and query_examples.py backfill historical data, so the service must be running with reject_client_timestamp_skew_s raised (see section 0).

1. Server monitoring

You want to record CPU, memory, and disk usage from several servers and query per-machine averages over the last hour. Each server sends readings with a host tag to distinguish them.

Send data (Python, one machine)

from sqtseries import Client
import psutil

c = Client()

while True:
    c.write("cpu.percent", psutil.cpu_percent(), {"host": "web1"})
    c.write("mem.percent", psutil.virtual_memory().percent, {"host": "web1"})
    c.write("disk.percent", psutil.disk_usage("/").percent, {"host": "web1"})
    time.sleep(10)

Send data (Go, another machine — no sqtseries installed)

// go get github.com/pebbe/zmq4
sock, _ := zmq.NewSocket(zmq.PUSH)
sock.Connect("tcp://192.168.1.10:12501")  // sqtseries is on this machine
sock.Send(`{"metric":"cpu.percent","value":42.0,"tags":{"host":"web2"}}`, 0)

Query the last hour of CPU

import time
from sqtseries import Client

c = Client()
now_ns = time.time_ns()
rows = c.query("cpu.percent", start=now_ns - 3600 * 10**9, end=now_ns,
               aggregation="avg", interval="1m")
for row in rows:
    print(f"Average CPU at {row['timestamp']}: {row['value']:.1f}%")

Note that the client takes nanosecond epochs for start/end; returned rows carry epoch- seconds timestamps.

Peak across all machines

stats = c.aggregate("cpu.percent", funcs=["avg", "max", "p95"])
print(f"Average: {stats['avg']:.1f}%, Max: {stats['max']:.1f}%, P95: {stats['p95']:.1f}%")

2. Instant dashboard (browser)

You want a web page that shows live readings the moment they arrive, and also displays how many other viewers are watching right now.

Live data feed (WebSocket)

const ws = new WebSocket("ws://127.0.0.1:12505/ws/subscribe?metric=sensor.");
ws.onmessage = (e) => {
    const point = JSON.parse(e.data);
    document.getElementById("latest").textContent =
        `${point.metric}: ${point.value}`;
};
// the service also sends {"type":"ping"} roughly every 30s — ignore it

Viewer count (admin socket)

Every 10 seconds, ask the admin socket how many WebSocket clients are connected:

import zmq, orjson, time

ctx = zmq.Context()
s = ctx.socket(zmq.REQ)
s.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:12504")

while True:
    s.send(orjson.dumps({"cmd": "connections"}))
    reply = orjson.loads(s.recv())
    print(f"Connected viewers: {len(reply.get('data', []))}")
    time.sleep(10)

Or subscribe to the stats PUB socket (port 12506) for a push-based alternative — see example 5 below.

3. Logging sensor data and running reports

You have 20 temperature sensors around a building, each writing once per minute. You want daily summary reports showing the minimum, maximum, and average per sensor.

Writing (this runs on each sensor's device)

from sqtseries import Client
c = Client()
c.write("temp.celsius", 19.2, {"room": "lobby", "floor": "1"})
c.write("temp.celsius", 22.7, {"room": "kitchen", "floor": "1"})
c.write("temp.celsius", 18.1, {"room": "basement", "floor": "-1"})

Daily report (run once a day from a script)

import time
from sqtseries import Client

c = Client()
now_ns = time.time_ns()
yesterday_ns = now_ns - 86400 * 10**9

rows = c.query("temp.celsius", start=yesterday_ns, end=now_ns,
               aggregation="avg", interval="1h")
# each row is one hour's average temperature across all sensors

# Or ask for the summary numbers directly:
stats = c.aggregate("temp.celsius", start=yesterday_ns, end=now_ns,
                    funcs=["avg", "min", "max", "count"])
print(f"Yesterday: avg={stats['avg']:.1f}, min={stats['min']:.1f}, "
      f"max={stats['max']:.1f}, readings={stats['count']}")

Which rooms are too hot?

Query the embedded engine directly when you need per-tag breakdowns (the wire protocol filters by metric, not by tag):

from sqtseries.engine import StorageEngine, create_sqlite_engine

engine = create_sqlite_engine("~/.sqtseries/data/db.sqlite")
store = StorageEngine(engine)

# group every series_id by its room tag
rooms = {}
for sid in store.series_ids_for_metric("temp.celsius"):
    _, tags_json = store.get_series_meta(sid)
    tags = orjson.loads(tags_json) if tags_json else {}
    rooms.setdefault(tags.get("room", "unknown"), []).append(sid)

# query each room separately
for room, sids in sorted(rooms.items()):
    rows = list(store.query_time_range(
        series_ids=sids, start_ns=yesterday_ns, end_ns=now_ns))
    avg = sum(v for _, v in rows) / len(rows) if rows else 0
    print(f"{room}: {avg:.1f} °C")

4. Alerting on anomalies

You want to know instantly when a reading goes outside normal bounds. You subscribe to the live stream and check every value as it arrives.

Python subscriber that alerts

from sqtseries import Client

c = Client()
THRESHOLD = 90.0  # alert if CPU goes above 90%

for payload in c.subscribe("cpu."):
    if payload is None:   # idle heartbeat
        continue
    value = payload["value"]
    if value > THRESHOLD:
        print(f"ALERT: {payload['metric']} = {value}% "
              f"on {payload['tags']['host']}")

ZMQ subscriber (Go — no Python needed)

sub, _ := zmq.NewSocket(zmq.SUB)
sub.Connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:12503")
sub.SetSubscribe("cpu.")

for {
    msg, _ := sub.RecvMessage(0)
    if len(msg) >= 2 {
        fmt.Println("ALERT:", string(msg[1]))
    }
}

5. Monitoring connections (admin + stats socket)

You want to know at all times how many clients are connected, which topics they are watching, and whether a specific device is still online.

Quick check: who is connected right now?

from sqtseries import Client
c = Client()
reply = c.admin("connections")
for conn in reply["data"]:
    print(f"{conn['id']}: {conn['kind']} from {conn['peer']} "
          f"watching {conn['topic']}")

Is this specific device still connected?

# You saved a connection ID when the WebSocket first connected:
device_id = "a1b2c3d4e5f6"

reply = c.admin("conncheck", ids=[device_id])
if device_id in reply["present"]:
    print("Device is online")
else:
    print("Device has disconnected")

How many subscribers does each topic have?

reply = c.admin("subscribers")
for sub in reply["subscriptions"]:
    print(f"{sub['topic']}: {sub['subscribers']} listeners")

Live stats feed (PUB socket subscription)

The stats PUB socket (port 12506) emits events in real time — no polling needed. Subscribe with a prefix to receive only what you care about:

import zmq, orjson

ctx = zmq.Context()
stats = ctx.socket(zmq.SUB)
stats.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:12506")
stats.setsockopt(zmq.SUBSCRIBE, b"conn")  # only connection events

while True:
    event_type, payload = stats.recv_multipart()
    data = orjson.loads(payload)
    if data.get("connected"):
        print(f"CONNECTED: {data['id']} from {data['peer']} "
              f"({data['kind']})")
    else:
        print(f"DISCONNECTED: {data['id']}")

Subscribe to b"sub" for ZMQ subscription events, or b"" for all events including the periodic report (every 10 seconds: uptime_s, ws_connections, zmq_subscribers, active_topics).

6. Data retention and cleanup

You want to keep the last 30 days of detailed data but drop anything older. By default this happens automatically — no configuration needed. To change the window or disable it:

# config.toml
[retention]
enabled = true
default_ttl = "90d"      # keep 90 days instead of 30
check_interval = "1h"    # check every hour

When a partition's data is entirely older than the TTL, its table and all associated rollup rows are dropped in one operation (DROP TABLE, whole monthly partition at a time). The pages are freed to SQLite's internal freelist and reused by new data, but the file itself keeps its peak size until you run sqtseries vacuum — see Backup & Restore for how vacuum works and when to run it.

Manual cleanup on demand

# Check current storage:
sqtseries stats

# Shrink the file (stop the service first for a full VACUUM):
sqtseries stop
sqtseries vacuum

# Or run ANALYZE to refresh query-plan statistics while running:
sqtseries optimize

7. High-rate ingestion

You are logging millions of rows and need the fastest possible write path. Batch your measurements and send them over ZeroMQ.

import zmq, orjson
import time, random

ctx = zmq.Context()
sock = ctx.socket(zmq.PUSH)
sock.setsockopt(zmq.SNDHWM, 10000)
sock.setsockopt(zmq.LINGER, 500)
sock.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:12501")

# Generate and send 100,000 points as fast as possible
start = time.monotonic()
for i in range(100_000):
    sock.send(orjson.dumps({
        "metric": "throughput.test",
        "value": random.random(),
        "tags": {"batch": str(i % 100)},
    }))
sock.close(linger=0)

elapsed = time.monotonic() - start
print(f"sent 100,000 points in {elapsed:.1f}s "
      f"({100_000 / elapsed:.0f} pts/sec)")

What to expect: the service commits one transaction per message (no app-level batching on the live path), so keep high-rate senders on the same fast network or use multiple senders — the PUSH HWM (10,000) acts as backpressure. Engine-level numbers (batched executemany inserts via scripts/benchmark.py, ~65–253K rows/s on an NVMe machine) are higher than what the one-message-at-a-time service path sustains; and output reliably on your own hardware with python3 scripts/benchmark.py.

8. Health check for load balancers

You want your load balancer or monitoring tool to know if sqtseries is healthy. Two options — CLI and HTTP:

# CLI: exits 0 if the database passes its check
sqtseries health
echo $?  # 0 = healthy, 1 = degraded

# HTTP: returns JSON (status + version only)
curl http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/health
# {"status":"ok","version":"0.1.0"}

# ZMQ admin (inside a Python health check):
from sqtseries import Client
c = Client()
h = c.admin("health")
if h["status"] == "ok" and h["database"] is True:
    print("healthy")

The HTTP health endpoint runs a quick_check on the SQLite file — it is not just a port check. If the database file is corrupted, the endpoint returns {"status":"degraded"}. Use it in your load balancer's health check configuration.

The question catalog — four canonical questions

The repo's examples/question_examples.py answers 13 questions; the four most common ones are shown below, each over the Python client (nanosecond epochs, aggregate(funcs=…)) and over HTTP with curl (second epochs, funcs=…). Timestamps differ by API: the HTTP gateway takes epoch seconds, the ZMQ client takes epoch nanoseconds. The values in the sample responses are illustrative shapes from the seeded demo data, not measured outputs.

Q1. Average CPU load over the last hour

import time
from sqtseries import Client

c = Client()
now_ns = time.time_ns()
avg = c.aggregate("cpu.load", start=now_ns - 3600 * 10**9, end=now_ns,
                  funcs=["avg"])["avg"]
print(f"Answer: {avg:.2f}")

now=$(date +%s)
curl "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=cpu.load&start=$((now-3600))&end=$now&funcs=avg"
# {"status":"ok","aggregations":{"avg":52.3}}

Q2. Peak temperature yesterday

import time
from sqtseries import Client

c = Client()
day_ns = (time.time() // 86400) * 86400 * 10**9               # UTC midnight today
peak = c.aggregate("temp.celsius",
                   start=day_ns - 86400 * 10**9, end=day_ns,
                   funcs=["max"])["max"]
print(f"Answer: {peak:.2f} °C")

now=$(date +%s)
yesterday=$((now / 86400 * 86400 - 86400))   # UTC midnight yesterday
today=$((now / 86400 * 86400))               # UTC midnight today
curl "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=temp.celsius&start=$yesterday&end=$today&funcs=max"
# {"status":"ok","aggregations":{"max":24.5}}

Q3. p99 response time over the past week

import time
from sqtseries import Client

c = Client()
now_ns = time.time_ns()
p99 = c.aggregate("latency.web", start=now_ns - 7 * 86400 * 10**9, end=now_ns,
                  funcs=["p99"])["p99"]
print(f"Answer: {p99:.0f} ms")

now=$(date +%s)
curl "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=latency.web&start=$((now - 7*86400))&end=$now&funcs=p99"
# {"status":"ok","aggregations":{"p99":107.0}}

p99 (like median/p95) is served from raw rows — it has no rollup fast path. avg/sum/ min/max/count over wide windows use the hourly rollup automatically when the window spans completed hours.

Q4. How many measurements were recorded today?

import time
from sqtseries import Client

c = Client()
day_start_ns = (time.time() // 86400) * 86400 * 10**9
count = c.aggregate("visitors.web", start=day_start_ns, end=time.time_ns(),
                    funcs=["count"])["count"]
print(f"Answer: {count:.0f} readings")

now=$(date +%s)
day=$((now / 86400 * 86400))
curl "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=visitors.web&start=$day&end=$now&funcs=count"
# {"status":"ok","aggregations":{"count":288.0}}

Run python3 examples/question_examples.py to see all 13 questions answered end to end against a seeded instance.
